tip: 내일 (naeil = tomorrow) takes no time particle – 시장에 (sijang-e) keeps its 에, but 오늘 (oneul), 내일, and 지금 (jigeum) never take 에.
에서 (eseo) marks where an action happens: 도서관에서 공부해요 (doseogwan-eseo gongbuhaeyo = I study at the library). Plain 에 (e) only marks going to or being at a place.
'Like' is 좋아해요 (joahaeyo) with 를 (reul): 커피를 좋아해요 (keopi-reul joahaeyo = I like coffee). 좋아요 (joayo) without 하 (ha) means 'is good' instead.
In 'where is X?' questions X takes 이/가 (i/ga): 지하철역이 어디에 있어요? (jihacheollyeok-i eodi-e isseoyo?) – 이/가 presents it as new to the conversation.
Korean has a single verb for 'is not there': 없어요 (eopseoyo). 열쇠가 여기에 없어요 (yeolsoe-ga yeogi-e eopseoyo = the key isn't here) – no 'is' + 'not' combo.
맛있어요 (masisseoyo = delicious) is literally 'taste exists': 맛 (mat = taste) + 있어요 (isseoyo = there is). So 불고기가 맛있어요 (bulgogi-ga masisseoyo) = the bulgogi has taste.
Koreans say 우리 집 (uri jip = our house) even for a home they live in alone – 우리 (uri) covers home, family, and country. 제 집 (je jip = my house) sounds oddly distant.
Position words come after their noun: 은행 앞에 (eunhaeng ap-e, literally 'bank front-at') – the reverse of English 'in front of the bank'.
